current_activity: providing armoured support during the Juno landings
notes: Brigade-level (below stated scope; included for context). An independent armoured brigade, not an organic part of the 3rd Canadian Division: Wikipedia lists it among the independent brigades and says it was assigned to British Second Army in January 1944, and it landed on 6 June with the 3rd Canadian Infantry Division, under its command for the assault (Wikipedia; Veterans Affairs Canada names the division and the brigade together as the designated assault formations). Its regiments were usually tasked individually to infantry units. 1st Hussars attacked Le Mesnil-Patry 11 June. [Review: parent_unit_id stays the 3rd Canadian Division (operational parent, now relationship attached); organic parent is now Second Army (was the 3rd Canadian Division); current_activity reworded from 'landing at Juno Beach in support of 3rd Canadian Division'; confidence raised from 0.5 to 0.7 by the rubric (approximate location, two source families: Wikipedia and Veterans Affairs Canada). Wikipedia's First Canadian Army page says the division and brigade were detached from that army to British I Corps for the assault; that standing link is not modelled because the army was not in Normandy on this date.]

location_qualifier: mainly the 6th Armoured Regiment (1st Hussars) with the Queen's Own Rifles
current_activity: attacks from Norrey-en-Bessin towards Le Mesnil-Patry with the Queen's Own Rifles at short notice; repulsed
notes: Event date: 11 June 1944, 1 p.m. (Stacey, p. 139; Ellis, vol. I, p. 253). Event definition: Ordered to clear the Mue valley, the brigade attacks on 11 June at very short notice, the orders having reached it only that morning; the 6th Armoured Regiment (1st Hussars), with the Queen's Own Rifles riding on its tanks, passes through Norrey-en-Bessin and deploys in the cornfields north of Le Mesnil-Patry under fire, and the attack fails with heavy loss (Ellis, vol. I, pp. 252-253; Stacey, p. 139). Wikipedia calls the battle a partial success with severe losses. Event support: three source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Stacey, the Canadian official history, and Wikipedia). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 253: "Unfortunately orders did not reach the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade and their associates The Queen's Own Rifles till the morning of the 11th"; "they deployed in the open cornfields north of le Mesnil Patry"; Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 139: "Planning begun on 10 June for an enterprise by the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade south of Norrey-en-Bessin"; Wikipedia, 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade: "the Battle of Le Mesnil-Patry on 11 June 1944, ended with only a partial success and severe losses to the Canadians". Location: Le Mesnil-Patry (PL0221) with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is the village, the objective; the fighting was in the fields north of it. Location support: Ellis, Stacey and Wikipedia name Le Mesnil-Patry. Commander: Brigadier R. A. Wyman (Stacey, pp. 139 and 216), wounded on 8 August 1944 (Stacey, p. 237). Context: Relationship: under the 3rd Canadian Division (existing relation from D-Day) and I Corps as that division's corps, start = row date (inferred value). The brigade's relation to Second Army from 6 June is closed the day before (inferred value), the brigade now being recorded with a corps.

current_activity: Atlantic: tanks of the 1st Hussars support the 8th Brigade against Colombelles and Giberville
notes: Event date: 18 July 1944 (Stacey, pp. 171 and 173: "the morning of the 18th"; Ellis, vol. I, p. 343). Event definition: In Operation Atlantic the 8th Brigade of the 3rd Canadian Division, supported by the brigade, moves off from near Ranville at 7.45 a.m. against the factory area of Colombelles (Ellis, vol. I, p. 343); assisted by tanks of the 1st Hussars, the Queen's Own Rifles clear the cross-roads east of Colombelles and move on Giberville (Stacey, p. 171). The brigade is under II Canadian Corps, which took over its front on 11 July (Stacey, p. 166). Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Stacey, the Canadian official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 343: "Starting from near Ranville at 7.45 a.m., the leading brigade (8th) of the 3rd Canadian Infantry Division with support from the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade had moved against the factory area of Colombelles"; Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 171: "Assisted by tanks of the 1st Hussars, the Queen's Own cleared the area of the cross-roads east of Colombelles"; p. 173: "on the morning of the 18th"; p. 166: "At 3:00 p.m. on 11 July it took over about 8000 yards of front in the Caen sector; with the 2nd and 3rd Canadian Infantry Divisions, the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade". Location: Colombelles, Calvados (PL0667) with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is the village; the brigade's tanks fought round the factory area and the cross-roads east of it. Location support: Ellis and Stacey name Colombelles. Commander: Brigadier R. A. Wyman (Stacey, pp. 139 and 216), wounded on 8 August 1944 (Stacey, p. 237).

current_activity: under the 2nd Canadian Division, helps beat off four counter-attacks between Point 67 and Saint-André-sur-Orne
notes: Event date: 21 July 1944, morning (Ellis, vol. I, p. 350: "the 21st"; Stacey, p. 175). Event definition: On 21 July the Germans attack the Canadian position on the east bank of the Orne from Point 67 to Saint-André early in the morning; four attacks are beaten off by half past ten with the help of the artillery and of the brigade, which has been put under the 2nd Canadian Division and makes the German tanks pay heavily (Ellis, vol. I, p. 350). Stacey says General Simonds assigned the brigade to the 2nd Division to secure his right flank (p. 175). Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Stacey, the Canadian official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 350: "Four separate attacks were beaten off by half past ten that morning with the help of the artillery, and of the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade which had now been put under the command of the 2nd Division"; Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 175: "and the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade was assigned to the 2nd Division". Location: Saint-André-sur-Orne, Calvados (new place) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is Saint-André, one end of the position named; the position ran to Point 67, about 2 km away. Location support: Ellis names the position from Point 67 to Saint-André (p. 350). Commander: Brigadier R. A. Wyman (Stacey, pp. 139 and 216), wounded on 8 August 1944 (Stacey, p. 237). Context: Relationship: attached to the 2nd Canadian Division (Ellis, p. 350; Stacey, p. 175), start = row date (inferred value); the 3rd Canadian Division attachment is closed the day before (inferred value).

location_qualifier: less the 1st Hussars; with the 4th Infantry Brigade under command
current_activity: Totalize: Wyman's assault force crosses the start line west of the Falaise road in four armoured columns at 11.30 p.m.
notes: Event date: 7 August 1944, 11.30 p.m. (Ellis, vol. I, p. 420). Event definition: In the opening attack of Operation Totalize, the 2nd Canadian Division with the brigade attacks west of the Falaise road, crossing the line between Soliers and Saint-André-sur-Orne at 11.30 p.m. on 7 August (Ellis, vol. I, p. 420); General Foulkes has put the assault force under Brigadier Wyman: his brigade (less the 1st Hussars) with the 4th Infantry Brigade in armoured carriers and the 8th Reconnaissance Regiment, in four tight columns (Stacey, p. 216; Ellis, p. 421). Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Stacey, the Canadian official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 420: "by the 2nd Canadian Division with the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade west of it"; "Crossing a line between Soliers and St. André sur Orne at 11.30 p.m. on August the 7th"; Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 216: "General Foulkes had placed the assault force on his front under the command of Brigadier Wyman of the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade". Location: Saint-André-sur-Orne, Calvados (new place) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the western end of the start line; the columns advanced south from it during the night, so the precision is 10 km. Location support: Ellis names the start line between Soliers and Saint-André (p. 420). Commander: Brigadier R. A. Wyman (Stacey, pp. 139 and 216), wounded on 8 August 1944 (Stacey, p. 237).

current_activity: Undergo: supports the 3rd Canadian Division's attack on Calais
notes: Event date: 25 September 1944 (Ellis, vol. II, p. 65). Event definition: On 25 September the 3rd Canadian Division, less one brigade, attacks Calais, supported by the brigade and by Flails, AVREs and Crocodiles of the 31st Tank Brigade of the 79th Armoured Division (Ellis, vol. II, p. 65); General Spry's plan used the 7th and 8th Brigades assisted by the brigade (Stacey, p. 348). Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Stacey, the Canadian official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 65: "On September the 25th the attack by the 3rd Canadian Infantry Division less one brigade was supported by the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade"; Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 348: "General Spry planned to attack Calais with the 7th and 8th Infantry Brigades, assisted by the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade". Location: Calais, Pas-de-Calais (PL0678) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the town; the brigade supported attacks on the outer defences round it, so the precision is 10 km. Location support: Ellis and Stacey name Calais. Commander: Brigadier J. F. Bingham, commander after Brigadier Wyman was wounded on 8 August 1944 (Stacey, p. 237). Context: Relationship: attached to the 3rd Canadian Division for the attack (Ellis; Stacey), start = row date (inferred value); II Canadian Corps continues (inferred value: the sources read give no change).

current_activity: within a few miles of Breda; put under the Polish Armoured Division to drive for Moerdijk
notes: Event date: 27 October 1944, nightfall (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 125-126). Event definition: By nightfall on 27 October, in I Corps' advance north, the 1st Polish Armoured Division is attacking Breda from the flank and the brigade has got within a few miles of Breda; the same day I Corps orders the Poles, with the brigade under command, to drive for Moerdijk and its Maas bridges (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 125-126). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 125: "at the same time the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade had got to within a few miles of Breda"; p. 126: "The Poles, with the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade under command, were to drive ahead for Moerdijk". Location: Breda, Noord-Brabant (PL0623) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is Breda; the brigade was a few miles short of it, so the precision is 10 km. Location support: Ellis says the brigade was within a few miles of Breda (p. 125). Context: Relationship: I Corps, whose orders of 27 October put the brigade under the 1st Polish Armoured Division (Ellis, p. 126); both start on the row date (inferred value); the II Canadian Corps relation and the 3rd Canadian Division attachment are closed the day before (inferred value).

current_activity: Blockbuster: two regiments support the 2nd Canadian Division astride the Goch-Calcar road on the Calcar ridge
notes: Event date: 26 February 1945, 4.30 a.m. (Stacey, p. 492). Event definition: Opening Operation Blockbuster at 4.30 a.m. on 26 February, the 2nd Canadian Division, with two regiments of the brigade, puts two brigades astride the road from Goch where it climbs the ridge south of Calcar (Stacey, p. 492). Ellis lists the brigade in II Canadian Corps when Veritable opened (vol. II, p. 255). Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Stacey, the Canadian official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 255: "When Veritable opened II Canadian Corps consisted of: 49th Infantry Division, 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade"; Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 492: "Striking at 4:30 a.m. on the 26th, General Matthews, with the support of two regiments of the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade". Location: Calcar (Kalkar), North Rhine-Westphalia (PL0705) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is Calcar; the attack was on the ridge south of the town, so the precision is 10 km. Location support: Stacey names the Goch road on the ridge south of Calcar (p. 492). Context: Relationship: II Canadian Corps (Ellis, vol. II, p. 255; Stacey); the regiments support the 2nd Canadian Division, recorded as attached from the row date (inferred value); the Polish attachment of October is closed the day before (inferred value).
